did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 2 of Lamentations is structured as an alphabetical acrostic: its verses begin in the order of the letters א–ת. The first verse describes the downfall of Daughter Zion, who is portrayed as having been cast from heaven to earth, while Israel’s glory was humiliated on the day of the LORD’s anger.

Did you know? In this verse, the LORD is figuratively described as holding a bow and standing like an enemy, emphasizing the force of the attack: all the precious things of the city—that is, its finest and most beautiful people—were killed.

Did you know? The destruction is described as the demolition of a booth or garden, while it is also said that festivals and Sabbaths were forgotten in Zion. The verse therefore connects the destruction of the place with the end of worship and festival life.

Did you know? The collapse of the system of leadership and guidance is described here: the king and princes are among the nations, there is no law, and the prophets no longer receive visions from the LORD.

Did you know? The mourning practices mentioned in this verse are sitting silently on the ground, putting dust on one’s head, and wearing sackcloth. Both the elders of Daughter Zion and the young women of Jerusalem are described as sharing in the mourning.

Did you know? The mourner also describes the disaster through physical reactions: his eyes are exhausted from tears, his insides churn, and his liver is poured out on the ground. His personal anguish is presented as part of the national suffering of my people.

Did you know? The magnitude of the disaster is described through questions with no answer: nothing can be compared with Jerusalem’s suffering, and no comfort or healing is sufficient for the great wound, as vast as the sea.
Did you know? The criticism of the prophets is not only that they proclaimed false and empty visions, but also that they did not expose the people’s guilt or lead them to repentance and restoration.

Did you know? Daughter Zion is called to turn her weeping into continual prayer: to let her tears flow like a stream day and night and not allow her eyes to cease. The cry is directed straight to the LORD.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the enemy is summoned from every side as on a festival day, but unlike a joyful festival, there is no survivor or remnant. The lament thus concludes with a description of the complete destruction of young and old, and of everyone the city had raised.
